clinicalScope: Collagen disorders (genetic and acquired connective‑tissue diseases) in adult patients presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Collagen Disorders
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Collagen is the body’s main structural protein, giving strength to skin, bone, vessels and organs. Defects or excess of collagen cause a range of inherited and acquired diseases that affect many systems, especially in settings with limited diagnostic tools.

sections.p: Collagen forms the scaffold of the extracellular matrix (ECM), providing tensile strength, supporting cell adhesion, and guiding tissue repair. Its integrity is essential for organ function and wound healing.
b: Most abundant protein (~30% of total body protein)
Exists as 28 genetically distinct types; Types I, III, and V are fibrillar, Type IV forms basement membranes
Triple‑helix structure (Gly‑X‑Y) confers stability
Vitamin C‑dependent hydroxylation is critical; deficiency → scurvy

sections.p: Each collagen molecule is a triple helix of three α‑chains; post‑translational modifications create cross‑links that determine tissue‑specific strength.
b: Glycine every third residue allows tight helix packing
Proline and hydroxyproline stabilize the helix via hydrogen bonds
Lysyl oxidase (copper‑dependent) creates aldehyde groups for covalent cross‑linking
Glycosylation of hydroxylysine residues aids fibril assembly

sections.h: Pathway or mechanism step by step
sections.p: Collagen synthesis proceeds from gene transcription to extracellular fibril formation.
b: 1. Transcription of COL genes → pre‑pro‑α‑chains in rough ER
2. Signal peptide removal → pro‑α‑chains; three chains assemble into procollagen triple helix
3. Prolyl‑4‑hydroxylase and lysyl‑hydroxylase (vitamin C, Fe²⁺, O₂) hydroxylate proline/lysine
4. Glycosyltransferases add glucose/galactose to hydroxylysine
5. Procollagen secreted; N‑ and C‑propeptides cleaved by procollagen N‑ and C‑proteinases
6. Tropocollagen self‑assembles into fibrils; lysyl oxidase cross‑links fibrils

sections.p: Key enzymes are tightly regulated; deficiencies produce characteristic clinical pictures.
b: Prolyl‑4‑hydroxylase – requires vitamin C, Fe²⁺, O₂; scurvy when impaired
Lysyl‑hydroxylase – also vitamin C dependent; affects cross‑linking
Lysyl oxidase – copper‑dependent; deficiency leads to weak connective tissue
Procollagen N‑ and C‑proteinases – cleave propeptides; mutations cause Ehlers‑Danlos type VII

sections.p: Collagen turnover balances synthesis and degradation via matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) and their inhibitors (TIMPs).
b: TGF‑β up‑regulates COL1A1/2 transcription; over‑activity → fibrosis
MMP‑1 (collagenase) degrades fibrillar collagen; inhibited by TIMP‑1
Inflammatory cytokines (IL‑1, TNF‑α) increase MMP activity, causing tissue breakdown
Hypoxia induces lysyl oxidase, promoting cross‑linking in wound scar

sections.p: Collagen synthesis consumes ATP, vitamin C, iron, copper and requires adequate protein intake; malnutrition impairs wound healing.
b: Each hydroxylation step uses one O₂ and one α‑ketoglutarate → succinate
Copper deficiency reduces lysyl oxidase activity → weak vessels
Protein‑energy malnutrition lowers pro‑α‑chain production
Chronic infection (TB, HIV) can dysregulate TGF‑β, predisposing to fibrosis

sections.p: Both inherited defects and acquired dysregulation of collagen produce recognizable syndromes.
b: Osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1/2 mutation) – brittle bones, blue sclerae
Ehlers‑Danlos syndrome (COL3, COL5, COL1 variants) – hyper‑extensible skin, joint laxity, vascular rupture risk
Alport syndrome (COL4A5 mutation) – hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss, ocular anomalies
Systemic sclerosis (autoimmune) – excessive collagen deposition → skin tightening, pulmonary fibrosis
Rheumatoid arthritis – MMP‑mediated collagen breakdown in joints

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, simple tests can hint at collagen pathology; definitive diagnosis often needs specialized assays.

t.b: Detects deficiency causing impaired hydroxylation; <0.2 mg/dL suggests scurvy
Measures bone collagen turnover; elevated in osteogenesis imperfecta
Identifies abnormal collagen fibril diameter in Ehlers‑Danlos; not routinely available
Supports systemic sclerosis; positive in ~30 % diffuse disease

sections.p: Complications arise from both insufficient and excessive collagen.
b: Fractures and hearing loss in osteogenesis imperfecta
Arterial rupture, organ perforation in vascular Ehlers‑Danlos
Progressive renal failure in Alport syndrome
Pulmonary hypertension from systemic sclerosis‑related fibrosis
Joint deformities and disability in severe rheumatoid arthritis

sections.p: Management targets the underlying defect, modulates collagen turnover, and prevents complications.
b: Bisphosphonates (e.g., pamidronate) for osteogenesis imperfecta to increase bone density
Beta‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) for vascular Ehlers‑Danlos to reduce arterial stress
ACE inhibitors or ARBs for early renal protection in Alport syndrome
Immunosuppression (methotrexate, mycophenolate) for systemic sclerosis when organ involvement progresses

sections.p: Misinterpretation of collagen‑related signs can lead to delayed or inappropriate care.
b: Attributing easy bruising solely to thrombocytopenia; consider vascular Ehlers‑Danlos
Confusing joint hyper‑mobility from physiotherapy with Ehlers‑Danlos; use Beighton criteria
Assuming all restrictive lung disease is asthma; check for systemic sclerosis‑related fibrosis
Relying on normal serum calcium to rule out bone disease; collagen defects affect bone matrix independent of calcium

sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, key investigations, and rational management steps.
b: Identify the collagen type involved from clinical distribution (e.g., Type IV → kidney/ear/eye)
Use bedside clues: skin translucency, joint laxity, fracture history
Prioritise inexpensive tests (vitamin C, urine protein) when advanced assays unavailable
Formulate a step‑wise plan: correct deficiency → protect organ function → monitor complications

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden massive hemoptysis in systemic sclerosis (possible pulmonary hypertension crisis)
Spontaneous arterial rupture or massive gastrointestinal bleed in vascular Ehlers‑Danlos
Rapid decline in renal function with hematuria in Alport syndrome

faq.q: Why does vitamin C deficiency cause bleeding gums?
faq.a: Without vitamin C, prolyl‑hydroxylase cannot hydroxylate proline, leading to unstable collagen and fragile capillary walls.

faq.q: How can I differentiate joint hyper‑mobility from Ehlers‑Danlos?
faq.a: Use the Beighton score and look for skin hyper‑extensibility, easy bruising, and family history; isolated hyper‑mobility without skin changes is usually benign.

faq.q: Is collagen supplementation useful in these disorders?
faq.a: Oral collagen peptides are not incorporated into native collagen; they do not correct genetic defects or improve tensile strength.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with translucent skin, hyper‑extensible joints and a history of spontaneous arterial rupture – which collagen type is defective and why is surgical repair high‑risk? — Type III collagen; vessels lack tensile strength, sutures may tear.

A child with blue sclerae, multiple fractures, and normal calcium levels – what is the most likely diagnosis and the key genetic abnormality? — Osteogenesis imperfecta; COL1A1 or COL1A2 mutation affecting type I collagen.

In a patient with progressive dyspnoea, skin tightening, and a positive anti‑Scl‑70, what pathophysiologic process explains the restrictive lung pattern? — Excessive TGF‑β‑driven collagen deposition in the interstitium reduces lung compliance.

A patient with hematuria, sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities – which collagen defect is responsible and what is the inheritance pattern? — Type IV collagen defect (COL4A5); X‑linked recessive.
When vitamin C is unavailable, which clinical sign is most reliable for diagnosing scurvy in a malnourished adult? — Perifollicular hemorrhage with corkscrew hairs.

A 45‑year‑old man with rheumatoid arthritis develops a pleural effusion; what collagen‑related mechanism is most likely? — MMP‑mediated degradation of fibrillar collagen in the pleura leading to exudative effusion.

Why is lysyl oxidase activity reduced in patients with copper deficiency and what clinical manifestation may result? — Copper is a cofactor; deficiency leads to weak cross‑links, presenting as aneurysms or easy bruising.

In low‑resource settings lacking skin biopsy, how would you confirm a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers‑Danlos? — Apply the revised Villefranche criteria: arterial/organ rupture, thin translucent skin, family history, and positive genetic testing if available.
What is the rationale for using ACE inhibitors in early Alport syndrome? — They reduce intraglomerular pressure, slowing progression of collagen‑based basement membrane damage.

A patient with systemic sclerosis has worsening Raynaud’s and new digital ulcers; which laboratory test would help assess disease activity and why might it be unavailable? — Serum anti‑Scl‑70; limited availability in many African labs, so rely on clinical scoring.

How does chronic HIV infection influence collagen turnover and what complication may arise? — HIV‑associated cytokines increase TGF‑β, promoting fibrosis; patients may develop restrictive lung disease or cardiac diastolic dysfunction.

During wound healing, why is collagen deposition delayed in malnourished patients and what simple intervention can improve outcomes? — Lack of amino acids and vitamin C impairs hydroxylation; providing protein‑rich diet and vitamin C supplementation accelerates healing.
